meta.tagline: The free-spirited city of fog, hills and the orange bridge

pills: The fog has a name: Karl

overview.title: Welcome to San Francisco
overview.intro: San Francisco is a theater stage on seven hills: Victorian houses pose on the slopes, cable car bells have rung the same melody for one hundred fifty years, and the orange bridge performs its show slipping in and out of fog. This city has always hosted the extremes — gold rushers, beat poets, flower children and tech revolutionaries all met in the same seven square miles. Even the fog is a character: his name is Karl and he has a social media account. Bring a jacket, trust the hills — San Francisco tells many stories per mile.

local_word.definition: The name locals gave the San Francisco fog: Karl the Fog. In summer he slides through the Golden Gate in the afternoon and swallows the city, retreating by morning — instead of resenting him, the city named him and made him a joke. 'Karl's here' is a weather report; wrap up in your jacket and join the game.

rules.title: Don't trust summer: dress in layers
rules.description: In San Francisco, August is the month shivering tourists buy fleece: Karl arrives in the afternoon and the temperature drops ten degrees. The rule is simple — a jacket in every season, a layer in every bag. The 'California = warm' equation is void in this city.

rules.title: Buy the Alcatraz ticket weeks ahead
rules.description: Alcatraz tours are the city's best-selling ticket and sell out days or weeks in advance: buy early from the official site and never skip the audio tour — narrated by former inmates, it's among the world's best. The first morning boat adds island fog and silence as a bonus.

rules.title: Leave nothing in the car
rules.description: The city's known problem is car break-ins: even one visible bag is a risk. If driving, load the trunk before you park and prefer staffed garages — the visitor who follows this one rule has a trouble-free SF trip.

tip.label: The SF philosophy
tip.text: This city is measured in hills, not miles: a two-kilometer walk means three climbs, five views and two climates. Keep the plan small and accept the climb — every summit pays a panorama, and behind every fog waits a surprise.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: SF is compact but vertical: Muni and BART are the spine, the cable car a nostalgic feast, and walking a hill sport.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: From SFO the BART train reaches downtown in half an hour: cheap and painless. Ride apps run 25–45 minutes by traffic — at busy hours BART nearly always wins.

items.title: Cable car mastery
items.description: The cable car is working transit, not a museum piece: the Powell lines draw tourist queues, while the California line gives the same experience without one. Standing on the running board is the peak of the ride — hold on tight.

items.title: Muni and BART
items.description: The Muni metro-bus network covers the city, BART covers the bay: a Clipper card works on both. The historic F-line streetcars run vintage cars from the Castro to the Wharf — a nostalgia tour at transit fare.

items.title: The art of hill walking
items.description: SF is toured on foot, but the route is drawn cleverly: take the stairway streets (Filbert, Lyon) uphill and save the descents for views. Every hill is a neighborhood, every neighborhood another city.

items.title: Pedaling the bridge
items.description: The classic route: bike from the Wharf across the Golden Gate, descend into Sausalito, ferry back. The wind on the deck is serious — bring a snug jacket and two hours; 'bike the bridge, ferry back' is the city's best half day.

callout.label: Cable car tip
callout.text: Board the cable car on the California line: no queue, steep hills, the same view. If you must ride the Powell line, board at the turnaround at 08:00 — don't melt hours in the Union Square queue; the bell rings just as sweetly on every line.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In SF choosing a neighborhood means choosing a microclimate: the Mission's sun, North Beach's Italian soul, the Marina's bay breeze.

local_word.definition: The name for Victorian houses painted in three or more colors: the most famous line up in the 'postcard row' at Alamo Square. These wooden ladies who survived the earthquakes are the city's architectural identity — their facades are not decoration but a form of preservation. Look up on any walk: a few ladies pose on every street.

items.name: North Beach
items.description: The beat generation's bookstore, espresso bars and the lawns of Washington Square: SF's most characterful neighborhood. Walking distance to the cable car and the Wharf — the classic for atmosphere seekers.

items.name: The Mission
items.description: The city's sunniest microclimate: mural alleys, taquerías and vintage shops. Dolores Park's lawn is the city's living room on weekends — the young, colorful side.

items.name: Marina and Cow Hollow
items.description: A pastel neighborhood beside the Palace of Fine Arts and the bayside path: breakfast spots and boutiques. A Golden Gate-view running track at the door — the sporty, airy base.

items.name: Nob Hill and Union Square
items.description: The junction of the cable car lines, historic hotels and a central location: every connection passes through here. The hills are serious — the reward is views and practicality.

items.name: Hayes Valley
items.description: Boutiques, wine bars and the opera and symphony halls next door: SF's graceful small quarter. The Painted Ladies of Alamo Square within walking distance.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: SF's calendar runs backwards: the warmest months are September and October, the foggiest are midsummer — whoever knows Karl's schedule wins.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Clear Window
items.subtitle: Spring · Green hills, fresh skies
items.description: Winter rains have greened the hills and the air runs clear and mild: bridge views are sharp and crowds sit below summer levels. The Presidio and Marin trails live their finest season.

callout.label: April tip
callout.text: On an April morning climb into the Marin Headlands: green hills, a crystal bridge and the blue bay in one frame. Battery Spencer is generous to photographers at sunrise — a windbreaker is mandatory.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Karl's Stage
items.subtitle: Summer · Foggy afternoons, shivering tourists
items.description: Summer is fog season in SF: clear mornings, Karl on stage by afternoon. The Mission can bask while the bridge disappears — follow the microclimates and dress in layers. The crowds peak; the weather doesn't.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: In August the bridge photo is taken between 09:00 and 11:00: by afternoon Karl swallows the towers. The tourist who came in shorts buys fleece at the Wharf — bring your jacket; in this city, summer is a concept.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Locals' Summer
items.subtitle: Autumn · The year's warmest, clearest weeks
items.description: September and October are SF's true summer: Karl goes on vacation, temperatures peak, skies clear. Beach days, open-air festivals and sharp bridge views — the calendar's smartest choice.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: In early October take a late afternoon at Baker Beach: the bridge crystal, the sun warm, the crowds gone. If you catch Fleet Week, the Blue Angels perform above the bridge — the city's most cinematic weekend.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Rain and Greening
items.subtitle: Winter · Rain breaks, empty museums, greening hills
items.description: SF winter is mild and rainy: the breaks between storms run clear and photogenic, and the hills turn green. Museums are calm and hotels friendly — the season for seeing the city without crowds.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: On a post-rain afternoon walk the Lands End trail: rinsed air, giant waves and the bridge's dramatic frame. Sunset at the Sutro Baths ruins on the way back — winter SF's finest scene.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The SF table is a partnership of bay and migration: sourdough's crust, the burrito's heft, dim sum's steam and third-wave coffee.

local_word.definition: The giant burrito style born in the Mission district: rice, beans, meat, salsa and guacamole — a kilo of architecture wrapped in foil. Invented at taquería counters in the 1960s, it spread to the world from here. Eat it peeling the foil, forget the fork — Mission-style is not a meal but an oath of allegiance.

items.name: The Mission burrito
items.description: The giant foil-wrapped classic: al pastor or carne asada, the 'super' version with guacamole. The queue moves fast at the Mission's storied taquerías — decide before the counter, peel the foil layer by layer.

items.name: Sourdough and chowder
items.description: SF's sourdough is as old as the city — they say the starter feeds on the foggy air. Drink your clam chowder from a bread bowl beside the bay: touristy but legitimate.
items.tag: Fog-fed starter · in a bread bowl

items.name: The dim sum morning
items.description: America's oldest Chinatown and the Richmond's boulevards are dim sum heavens: steaming baskets chosen from the cart, fast counters. Char siu bao and har gow are your starting point.
items.tag: By the basket · choose from the cart

items.name: Dungeness crab
items.description: The bay's sweet-fleshed crab in season from November to June: steamed plain or garlic-butter style. The season's opening is a small city holiday — in season, don't hesitate.

items.name: The third-wave coffee pilgrimage
items.description: Coffee's third wave took shape in this city: single origins, pour overs and tasting bars. A morning tour of the neighborhood roasters — SF takes coffee seriously; so should you.

items.name: Buena Vista Irish coffee
items.description: Irish coffee entered America in 1952 across this bar's counter: the bartender lines up ten glasses at once for the show. The post-Wharf ritual — there may be a queue; the warm glass is worth it.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: Fisherman's Wharf's restaurant strip is the weakest link in the price-to-flavor chain: beyond a chowder bowl and a crab stand, carry your table to the neighborhoods. The Mission, the Richmond and Chinatown give twice the flavor on the same budget — a queued taquería never lies.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the bridge; these six are SF's wave-sounding, mosaic-stepped hidden face.

items.name: Sutro Baths and Lands End
items.description: The oceanside ruins of a once-vast swimming palace and the cliff trail above: waves, cypress trees and the bridge's distant frame. At sunset, SF's most dramatic corner.

items.name: The 16th Avenue Tiled Steps
items.description: 163 steps clad in a sea-themed mosaic: the pattern completes as you climb, and the ocean opens from the top. In the quiet Moraga Street neighborhood — loveliest in morning light.

items.name: The Marin Headlands
items.description: Old artillery batteries on the hills across the bridge: from Battery Spencer the towers fall into your lap with the city arrayed behind. By bike or car — the throne of the SF photograph.

items.name: Musée Mécanique
items.description: Hundreds of antique coin machines at the Wharf's edge: fortune-teller automatons, mechanical fairgrounds and cackling Laffing Sal. Entry free, tokens for pocket change — nostalgia's most entertaining museum.

items.name: Clarion Alley and Balmy Alley
items.description: The Mission's two mural alleys: political wall paintings, ever-changing layers and neighborhood stories. Pair with a taquería crawl — SF's conscience speaks on these walls.

items.name: Fort Point
items.description: The Civil War-era fort DIRECTLY under the Golden Gate: the steel span rises over the brick arches. Familiar from Hitchcock's Vertigo — and the best point for watching the surfers.

callout.label: Fog strategy
callout.text: SF's corners bargain with Karl: on foggy days the Musée Mécanique and the mural alleys, on clear days the Headlands and Lands End. Morning clarity is the surest window — schedule the big views before noon.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: SF's traps mostly grow from wrong expectations; know these four and see the city fog-free.

items.name: The 'California is warm' fallacy
items.description: The August tourist in shorts buys fleece in a 12°C wind at the Wharf: the SF summer is a microclimate joke.
items.instead: Dress in layers year-round and carry a windbreaker: don't let the morning sun fool you — Karl clocks in by afternoon. Plan knowing the warmest months are September and October.

items.name: Leaving Alcatraz to the last minute
items.description: The 'we'll buy tomorrow' tourist meets sold-out tickets or overpriced third-party 'combo tours'.
items.instead: Buy from the official seller weeks ahead; the early-morning and night tours are the atmospheric peak. Ticketless, a bay ferry passes near the island — better than nothing, but the real experience is on the rock.

items.name: Leaving belongings in the car
items.description: Window-smash theft is the city's chronic problem: even an empty bag on the seat means a glass bill.
items.instead: Leave NOTHING in the car — even the trunk counts as risky once you've parked; carry your things. Prefer staffed garages; best of all, go carless in the city and save the car for escapes like Muir Woods.

items.name: The Wharf restaurant strip
items.description: Fisherman's Wharf's neon restaurants sell mediocre seafood at view prices; a crowd is not proof of quality.
items.instead: At the Wharf, settle for a chowder bowl and a crab stand, and set the real table in the neighborhoods. For seafood, the storied kitchens of the Richmond and Chinatown always win.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In SF the costliest mistakes are planning mistakes: tickets early, jacket along, car empty. Solve those three and the city turns generous — the views are free, the hills are free exercise, and even Karl grows lovable in the end.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From cable car to bridge fog

steps.title: The California line cable car
steps.description: Board the queueless line and crest the hills to the bell: start the day on SF's 150-year-old rhythm.

steps.title: Dim sum in Chinatown
steps.description: Steaming baskets in America's oldest Chinatown: char siu bao for breakfast, then a walk down Grant Avenue.

steps.title: North Beach and City Lights
steps.description: Dive into the beat generation's bookstore, take an espresso break on Washington Square: the Italian quarter's calm hour.

steps.title: The Wharf and Musée Mécanique
steps.description: Watch the sea lions, play the coin machines, drink a chowder bowl facing the bay.

steps.title: Walk or pedal to the bridge
steps.description: Head from Crissy Field toward the bridge on foot or by bike: look up at the steel span from beneath, at Fort Point.

steps.title: Mission night
steps.description: A late tour of the mural alleys, then a super burrito and a neighborhood bar: close the day in the city's sunniest quarter.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Island, ocean and hills — the full SF

steps.title: Classic SF
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: cable car, dim sum, North Beach, the Wharf, the bridge, a Mission night.

steps.title: Alcatraz and the hills
steps.description: The first boat to Alcatraz (audio tour essential); a stall lunch at the Ferry Building; the Painted Ladies and Alamo Square's lawn in the afternoon; a wine bar and graceful dinner in Hayes Valley.

steps.title: Ocean day
steps.description: Golden Gate Park in the morning (Japanese garden + bison paddock); the 16th Avenue tiled steps at noon; the Lands End trail and a Sutro Baths sunset; the farewell close — an Irish coffee at the Buena Vista.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: SF speech is relaxed, wry and its own thing; these five phrases tune you to the city's frequency.

items.meaning: Very / a lot — the Bay Area's signature adverb: hear 'hella good', use it, earn a smile
The local name for San Francisco — never 'Frisco', even 'San Fran' is risky; 'The City' is safe harbor
The fog's name — 'Karl's out' means fog today; use his name and count as local
The two transit systems — 'I took BART' is part of the city's vocabulary
Excited, delighted — the official word of California optimism; use liberally

checklist.title: San Francisco Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Hella good! You've lived the city of fog and hills the way it deserves!
